title: Tagliatelle ai Funghi
subtitle: fresh mushroom and tagliatelle in cream and white wine
excerpt: Tagliatelle ai funghi is a northern Italian pasta with a simple sauce of sliced mushrooms, white wine, cream, and Parmesan. It is quick to make and suits chestnut mushrooms, dried porcini for depth, or a mix of wild mushrooms when in season. Serves 4.
sourceNotes: Tagliatelle ai funghi is a standard of Emilian home cooking. The combination of egg pasta with a mushroom and cream sauce has no single historical origin point but appears across Emilia-Romagna, Piedmont, and Veneto, wherever rich egg pasta and local porcini overlap. Pellegrino Artusi, La scienza in cucina (1891, public domain in Italy), includes a pasta with mushrooms using the porcini of the Apennines. The version with cream and white wine is a 20th-century Emilian elaboration that became one of the most widely cooked pasta dishes in northern Italian home kitchens.

glossaryTerms.definition: A flat, ribbon pasta from Emilia-Romagna, cut to about 8 mm width from a sheet of egg-enriched dough. Fresh tagliatelle (pasta all'uovo) is the standard for this sauce; dried egg tagliatelle works nearly as well. Plain dried pasta is a reasonable substitute.

content.text: ai funghi is northern Italian comfort food at its simplest. The mushrooms need to be cooked in two stages: first sauteed hard in butter until brown and the moisture has evaporated, then simmered in wine and cream until the sauce reduces to a coating consistency. The first stage is what most people skip, and it is the difference between mushrooms that taste sweet and concentrated and mushrooms that taste grey and soft.

A small handful of dried porcini, soaked and added with their liquid, makes chestnut mushrooms taste much better. If you can get fresh porcini, ceps, or chanterelles, use those instead. Wild mushrooms are more delicate, so reduce the cooking time.

items.prepNote: fresh egg tagliatelle (or dried egg tagliatelle)
soaked in 150 ml hot water 20 minutes, liquid strained
finely grated, plus extra to serve

content.text: If using dried porcini, soak them in 150 ml of hot water for 20 minutes. Lift out and chop roughly. Strain the liquid through a fine sieve and reserve.
Bring a large pot of well-salted water to the boil for the pasta.

Heat {{unsalted-butter}} of butter and {{olive-oil}} of olive oil in a large saute pan over a high heat. Add {{mushrooms-chestnut}} of sliced chestnut mushrooms in one layer. Do not stir immediately: let them brown on one side for 2 to 3 minutes, then turn. Cook until golden and the pan is dry. Add the soaked porcini if using.

Reduce the heat to medium. Add {{shallots}} of diced shallots and {{garlic}} of garlic. Cook for 2 minutes. Add {{dry-white-wine}} of white wine (and the strained porcini liquid if using) and let it bubble until mostly evaporated.

Add {{double-cream}} of double cream and thyme leaves if using. Simmer gently for 3 to 4 minutes until the cream thickens slightly. Season with {{sea-salt-fine}} of salt and {{black-pepper}} of black pepper.

Cook {{pasta-fresh}} of tagliatelle according to the packet. Reserve 100 ml of pasta water. Drain and add to the sauce pan. Toss to coat, adding pasta water if needed. Add {{parmesan}} of parmesan and {{parsley-flat}} of parsley and toss again. Serve in warm bowls with extra Parmesan.

items.symptom: Mushrooms release water and steam rather than browning
items.cause: Pan not hot enough, or too many mushrooms added at once
items.fix: Use a large pan and high heat. Cook in batches if needed. Crowded mushrooms steam; uncrowded mushrooms brown.
Add a splash of pasta cooking water and toss. The sauce should coat the pasta, not glue it together.

content.text: Tagliatelle ai funghi is from the part of Italy where the autumn porcini harvest and egg pasta meet: Emilia-Romagna, Piedmont, and the foothills of the Apennines. In the farmhouses of Emilia, tagliatelle with mushrooms and cream is as unremarkable and essential as roast chicken is in France. The cream is not lavish. It coats the pasta and carries the mushroom flavour. The dish is mild, filling, and forgiving of small variations in mushroom quality.
